summary: Teach that when you list ALL the possible outcomes of a trial — with no overlaps and nothing left out — their probabilities must total exactly 1. This lets a learner find a missing probability, or the probability of an event NOT happening, by subtracting from 1 (P(not A) = 1 − P(A)) instead of counting every unfavourable outcome. The reasoning only holds when the outcomes are mutually exclusive (no overlap) and exhaustive (cover everything).
misconceptions: Ignoring the sum-to-1 constraint and assigning a missing outcome an arbitrary or 'equal' value by analogy to another
Treating 'not A' as a single other outcome rather than everything except A, or thinking P(not A) equals P(A)
Adding probabilities of overlapping or non-exhaustive events and still expecting them to total 1
Adding fractions without a common denominator when totalling probabilities

activities.title: Fill the unit bar: the leftover IS the missing probability
steps: Take a bar exactly one unit long that stands for everything that can happen when you draw a counter from a bag of red, blue and green counters.
Set red to one-half of the bar and blue to one-sixth, marking those segments.
Before being told, work out what must fill the remaining strip and state it: green = 1 − (1/2 + 1/6) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3.
Mark 'P(not red)' by highlighting the entire rest of the bar (blue and green together) and give its value as 1 − P(red) = 1/2.
State in words why green could NOT be a free choice and why 'green must be 1/6 like blue' is wrong.
activities.insight: The whole of possibility has length 1; once some outcomes are placed, the leftover segment IS the missing probability, and 'not red' is the whole rest of the bar — everything except red — not a single other colour.

activities.title: Spinner that fills the whole disc
steps: Look at (or draw) a spinner whose coloured sectors must fill the entire disc with no gap and no overlap.
Given red = one-half and blue = one-third, predict the remaining sector's probability (yellow) before it is revealed: 1 − (1/2 + 1/3) = 1/6.
Check the revealed sector really is a sixth of the disc.
Tap or mark each sector in turn and track the running total as it reaches exactly 1.
activities.insight: A spinner's sectors are another model of the whole-equals-1 idea: because the sectors must fill the disc, the last sector's size (and probability) is forced by the others.

activities.title: Complement shortcut versus counting the others
steps: Calculate P(not rolling a 3) on a fair six-sided die two ways: first by subtracting, 1 − 1/6 = 5/6; then by counting all the other outcomes (1,2,4,5,6) and adding their probabilities (five sixths).
Compare the two methods, note they give the same answer, and that subtracting from 1 is faster when there are many unfavourable outcomes.
For the counter bag, find P(not red) as 1 − P(red) = 1/2 and confirm it matches blue + green (1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2).

Extend to a compound complement: a different bag of red, blue and green counters has P(red or blue) = 3/4; find P(green) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4, since each counter is exactly one of the three colours and the three colours exhaust the bag.
activities.insight: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) is a shortcut for 'everything except A', and it equals the sum of all the other outcomes because together they fill the whole; the same subtraction works when the known part is a compound event like 'red or blue'.

activities.title: Spot the impossible table
steps: Examine probability tables and decide which are impossible because the values do not total 1 (e.g. a table listing 1/2, 1/6 and 1/6 for three colours).
Add the values, compare the total with 1, and explain exactly what is wrong.
Correct one impossible table by finding the value that would make it total 1.
activities.insight: A complete list of outcomes that does not total 1 cannot be right. Checking the sum is a necessary test, but it is not enough on its own: a valid probability distribution also needs every value to be between 0 and 1, and the outcomes must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

activities.title: When the sum-to-1 argument does NOT apply: overlapping events
steps: Consider rolling a fair die and the events 'even' and 'prime'. List the outcomes for each: even = {2,4,6}, prime = {2,3,5}.
Notice that 2 belongs to both, so the events overlap and are NOT mutually exclusive.

Add P(even) = 3/6 and P(prime) = 3/6 and notice the total comes to 1 — then find the true chance of 'even or prime': the combined outcomes are {2,3,4,5,6}, which is 5/6, not 1. The naive sum reached 1 only by counting outcome 2 twice.
Explain why adding probabilities of overlapping events double-counts the shared outcome, so the total does not give P(even or prime), even when the arithmetic happens to land on 1.
Contrast with the counter-bag colours, which are mutually exclusive (a counter is exactly one colour) and exhaustive, so there the probabilities genuinely total 1.
activities.insight: Sum-to-1 and the complement shortcut only hold when the listed events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; with overlapping events, adding probabilities double-counts shared outcomes, and the total — even if it coincidentally equals 1 — does not represent the combined event.

activities.title: Socratic challenge: do your outcomes cover everything?
steps: Respond to prompts such as 'Do your outcomes cover everything, with no overlap?' and 'What do they add up to?'
Defend or revise a claim like 'so green must be 1/6 too' by appealing to the sum-to-1 constraint.
Explain in your own words why all the outcomes must add to exactly 1 — not more and not less.
activities.insight: Articulating the exhaustive-and-mutually-exclusive conditions and the total-equals-1 constraint strengthens reasoning beyond pattern-matching.

checkQuestion: A bag holds red, blue and green counters. P(red) = 1/2 and P(blue) = 1/6. A classmate says P(green) must be 1/6 as well, 'because green is just one colour, the same as blue'. Ask the child: is the classmate right? What is P(green), and why? Take the answer, then ask them to explain the reasoning fully (Tier 2).
checkAnswer: P(green) = 1/3. All the outcomes must total 1, so P(green) = 1 − (1/2 + 1/6) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3. The classmate is wrong: there is no rule that each colour is equally likely — the sum-to-1 constraint, not sameness with blue, fixes the missing value.
